questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a checklist "only as good as the understanding behind it"?
options: Because checklists are legally required to include a disclaimer in Salesforce projects
Because a checklist automatically becomes outdated after 90 days regardless of content

Because ticking a box without knowing why the item matters turns the checklist into theater instead of a real safeguard, since you won't recognize a variant of the same problem the checklist's exact wording doesn't cover
Because Salesforce prohibits using checklists during official code reviews
questions.explain: A checklist used as a retrieval aid for real understanding catches real problems; used mechanically without understanding why each item matters, it becomes a box-ticking exercise that misses anything slightly different from the checklist's literal wording.

questions.q: Which checklist category specifically addresses whether other triggers, Flows, or workflow rules on the same or related objects were considered, not just the code under direct review?
options: Transaction boundaries (Lesson 5)
Caching (Lesson 12)
Query optimization (Lesson 4)
Diagnosis readiness (Lessons 7-10)
questions.explain: The transaction boundaries category specifically calls for accounting for other automation sharing the same transaction, directly reflecting Lesson 5's lesson that governor limits are cumulative across everything running together, not just the code being reviewed.

questions.q: How does this checklist get used differently in a proactive design review versus a reactive live-incident response?
options: The checklist can only be used proactively; it has no reactive use at all

Proactively, it's used to ask "what will break at scale" before anything ships; reactively, it generates a fast hypothesis list of known anti-pattern categories to check against evidence already gathered during an incident
The checklist can only be used reactively, after an incident has already occurred
There is no difference; the checklist is applied identically regardless of context
questions.explain: The same checklist serves two purposes: catching problems before they ship (proactive design/code review) and quickly generating specific, testable hypotheses during a live incident (reactive troubleshooting per Lesson 10), rather than starting from nothing in either case.

questions.q: The checklist's "scalability" category (Lesson 6) specifically asks about which concern?
options: Whether every field in the object has a help text description
Whether the org has purchased the correct number of user licenses
Whether the Lightning page uses a two-column or three-column layout
Whether the design has been considered against future data volume, and whether it concentrates records on a single catch-all owner or parent by construction
questions.explain: The scalability checklist items directly mirror Lesson 6's two main concerns: designing against future (not just current) data volume, and avoiding catch-all records that create ownership or lookup skew as volume grows.

questions.q: What does the "diagnosis readiness" checklist category specifically check for?
options: Whether every Apex class has at least 75% code coverage
Whether the org's Salesforce edition supports Event Monitoring at all

Whether there's a way to capture a debug log or pull Event Monitoring data for a specific failing scenario if something does go wrong in production, rather than only having a vague bug report to work from
Whether a rollback plan exists for every deployment
questions.explain: Diagnosis readiness, drawn from Lessons 7-10, checks that the evidence-gathering tools (debug logs, Event Monitoring) are actually available and usable for a real production scenario, not just that code was written correctly.
